Li et al., 2020). Together with marine sediment records and ice cores, loess deposits, which contain the longest continuous terrestrial records, provide an important source of information for better understanding the evolution of regional/global paleoclimate systems over orbital to tectonic timescales (Liu, 1985; Porter & Zhisheng, 1995). The longest, thickest, and most detailed loess deposits are found on the Chinese Loess Plateau (CLP) in north-central China, where extensive research has been conducted to systematically investigate the evolution of the Asian monsoon, the aridification processes in the Asian interior, and the phased uplift of the Tibetan Plateau (An et al., 2001; F. H. Chen et al., 1997; J. Chen et al., 1999; Ding et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2002; W. Zhou et al., 2014). Loess deposits hold important paleoenvironmental significance and can also occur outside the CLP, such as those in northeastern China (Figure 1), which provide a key archive to assess intercorrelations across different regions. Notably, northeastern China is located on the margin of the area influenced by the Asian summer monsoon, which is highly sensitive to changes in monsoon intensity as well as high-latitude climate forcings, such as those associated with the westerlies (J. Chen et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2009; X. Zhou et al., 2016). Thus, the study of the loess deposits in northeastern China is promising for understanding the spatiotemporal evolution of the paleoclimate system in the Eurasian loess belt. Interpreting the climate proxies in the loess deposits, however, relies heavily on information from the dust sources (Chen & Li, 2011). For example, the grain size and flux of the aeolian dust recorded by loess deposits may not reflect the local climate if a distal dust source is considered (Ding et al., 2005; Yang & Ding, 2008). Changes in composition may also reflect changes in dust source rather than climate-driven wind sorting or post-depositional pedogenesis (J. Chen et al., 1999; Lu & An, 1998). In northeastern China, a compilation of Nd-Sr isotopic compositions indicates a specific source region for the loess, which is distinct from the loess on the CLP (Zeng et al., 2020) (Figure 2). The εNd (143Nd/144Nd ratio normalized by mantle value) and 87Sr/86Sr ratio of the loess in northeastern China (εNd: −6.9 to −9.7 and 87Sr/86Sr: 0.7108 to 0.7148) are similar to the material eroded from the Otindag Sandy Land (εNd: −15.0 to −4.4 and 87Sr/86Sr: 0.7096 to 0.7133) and the Horqin Sandy Land (εNd: −11.7 to −5.3 and 87Sr/86Sr: 0.7099 to 0.7133) that are proximal to the loess deposits in northeastern China (J. Chen et al., 2007; G. Li et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2020). The lack of dolomite in the loess in northeastern China is also consistent with the low carbonate content of these proximal arid lands (Lei et al., 2021; G. Li et al., 2007; Meng et al., 2019). However, discriminating dust sources among these potential proximal arid lands, especially the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land, remains difficult because these regions share similar lithological sources from the Central Asian Orogen. Thus, the (234U/238U) activity ratio of fine particles can serve as a source and age tracer. This method, here referred to as the uranium comminution age method, has been successfully applied to trace the production, transportation, and deposition of particles in various settings (Aciego et al., 2015; DePaolo et al., 2006; Handley et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2022; L. Li et al., 2018, 2019, 2022; Martin et al., 2019). Here, we use (234U/238U) and the comminution age method to study the provenance of the loess deposits in northeastern China. In this study, we measure the (234U/238U) activity ratio of a ∼1,000 ka-long loess-paleosol sequence in northeastern China and the surface sands in the potential upwind source areas (the Otindag Sandy Land, the Horqin Sandy Land, and the Hulun Buir Sandy Land) to better understand the source-to-sink transport process of aeolian dust in northeastern China. fetched_contents.text: Unraveling source-to-sink dust transport in Central and East Asia by identifying provenances of aeolian sediments Introduction The dust belt extending from the Sahara to the northwestern China and the Mongolia Plateau is a major dust-emitting region in the Northern Hemisphere (NH) (Engelbrecht and Derbyshire, 2010; Prospero et al., 2002; Shi et al., 2021). Mineral dust aerosols suspended in the atmosphere have had important effects in the Earth system (Kok et al., 2023). Therefore, a well-developed source-to-sink understanding of dust transport in this belt is a key issue to understand atmospheric and climate changes (Froyd et al., 2022; Kok et al., 2012; Shao et al., 2011) and long-term landscape evolution (Song et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2020). Asian source regions release dust to the atmosphere which is entrained and transported in suspension for long distance (Uno et al., 2009). It thereby provides a clearer picture of stepwise dust transport from source to sink. Enormous volumes of the silt- and clay-sized dust particles can accumulate as loess deposits in the downwind proximal regions, such as the Chinese Loess Plateau (An, 2000; Liu and Ding, 1998; Liu, 1985) and the foothills of high mountains in Central Asia (Dodonov, 1991; Li et al., 2015; Song et al., 2021; Song et al., 2014). Loess deposits have been intensively investigated as a unique terrestrial archive of paleo-dust flux on different timescales (An et al., 1991; Fitzsimmons et al., 2018; Frechen and Dodonov, 1998; Li et al., 2016a; Li et al., 2019b; Liu et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2006; Sun and An, 2005; Sun et al., 2010). Consequently, loess records help to improve prediction of environmental evolution and characterize dust cycling in Asia. Wind-blown fine (commonly ˂20 μm) grains in long-term suspension have a regional and even global-scale impact far beyond the source area (Gillette and Walker, 1977; Kok et al., 2012; Tegen and Lacis, 1996). In this sense, it is clearly necessary to ascertain the origin of fine-grained components of loess deposits and understand the wide-scale and long-term dust cycling in loess accumulation. High-altitude atmosphere over Eurasia prevails westerly airstreams (Fig. 1a, b, and Fig. S1). The large-scale high-altitude westerly airstreams have not only controlled spatial variations in precipitation across Eurasia (Aizen et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2016; Fohlmeister et al., 2017; Herzschuh et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2021; Luetscher et al., 2015; Nagashima et al., 2013; Perşoiu et al., 2019; Wassenburg et al., 2016), but also were thought to transport individual fine particles into downwind distant sinks in long-term suspension mode (Pye, 1987). For instance, based on end-member unmixing of loess grain size distribution, previous studies suggested that deposition of fine fractions with a mode size range of 2–10 μm in loess deposits on the CLP and in the northeast margin of Tibetan Plateau was linked to long-range transport of the high-level westerly airstreams (Nottebaum et al., 2014; Park et al., 2014; Prins and Vriend, 2007; Prins et al., 2007; Sun, 2004; Sun et al., 2004; Sun et al., 2008a; Vriend et al., 2011). Whereas, the origin of fine-grained component in loess is relatively complex, compared to coarse fraction (Li et al., 2022b). Pye (1987) indicated that the fine dust grains can also attach to larger grains for short-range transport. Furthermore, several studies attributed origin of the fine particles to transport of their silt- or sand-sized aggregates from proximal sources (Derbyshire et al., 1995; Falkovich et al., 2001; Mason et al., 2011; Mason et al., 2003; Pye, 1995; Qiang et al., 2010; Stevens and Lu, 2009; Újvári et al., 2016). The fine-grained materials can be also produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenic processes (Bland, 1998; Hao et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2006; Xiao et al., 1995). The controversial explanations to origin of the fine-grained components in loess deposits imply different transport mechanisms and pathways. Against this background, investigations into the origin of the fine (clay- and fine silt-sized) particles in turn facilitates to examine their potential links to the upper-level westerly airstreams. In this way, an improved framework for deciphering origins and transport patterns (or agents) of distal loess populations can be developed. Geochemical tracers, particularly trace elements and rare earth elements (REEs), have proved to be effective for distinguishing provenance of aeolian sediments and revealing their transport processes (Chen et al., 2022a; Chen et al., 2022b; Ferrat et al., 2011; Garzanti et al., 2020; Han et al., 2019; Hao et al., 2010; Hu and Yang, 2016; Jiang and Yang, 2019; Li et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2018b; Li et al., 2020d; Liu and Yang, 2018; Muhs, 2017; Muhs et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2022). Besides, SrNd isotopic compositions, which are determined at the time of crust-mantle differentiation, have also been extensively applied to trace the sources of aeolian sediments (Bird et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2007; Chen and Li, 2013; Dong et al., 2020; Rao et al., 2014; Rao et al., 2008; Rao et al., 2006; Sun, 2005; Wei et al., 2021; Xie and Chi, 2016; Xie et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021). fetched_contents.text: Strontium isotopes tracing of weathering processes and tidal mixing in a mountainous river system Introduction Riverine solutes play a pivotal role in global biogeochemical cycles, particularly in regulating ocean chemistry and atmospheric CO2 levels through continental weathering. Radiogenic strontium isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) have long been employed as powerful tracers for identifying the sources of dissolved materials in river systems due to their sensitivity to lithological heterogeneity (Capo et al., 1998; Probst et al., 2000; Jacobson et al., 2002; Bickle et al., 2005). The relative contributions of silicate versus carbonate weathering, catchment lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions together shape the spatial and temporal variations in riverine Sr concentrations and isotope ratios (Palmer and Edmond, 1992; Gaillardet et al., 1999). These variations, in turn, play a crucial role in controlling the global marine Sr isotope budget through riverine inputs to the oceans (Palmer and Edmond, 1989; Vance et al., 2009). Recent work on strontium stable isotope ratios (reported as δ88/86Sr) of terrestrial rocks, sediments, waters, and plants showed 88Sr-enrichment in river waters relative to their source rocks. Studies have attributed such isotopic fractionation to sorption onto secondary Fe/Mn oxides (Liu et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2024), incorporation into clay minerals (Stevenson et al., 2016; Su et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2024), precipitation and/or dissolution of carbonates (Liu et al., 2017; Shalev et al., 2017; Stevenson et al., 2024), and biological uptake by plants (de Souza et al., 2010; Bullen and Chadwick, 2016; Oeser and von Blanckenburg, 2020). Significant variations in δ88/86Sr values have been observed across river catchments (Krabbenhöft et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2013; Chao et al., 2015; Pearce et al., 2015; Andrews et al., 2016; Stevenson et al., 2018; Su et al., 2021; Stevenson et al., 2024) and in groundwater discharge zones (Mayfield et al., 2021; Ganguly et al., 2025), largely driven by these reactive geochemical processes. Building on this, several studies indicate that radiogenic and stable Sr isotopes in global river water are generally decoupled (Krabbenhöft et al., 2010; Pearce et al., 2015; Stevenson et al., 2018), with an exception reported under specific geological settings (e.g., the Xijiang River, China; Wei et al., 2013). Such decoupling becomes even more pronounced in estuarine and lagoonal environments, where carbonate precipitation-dissolution can strongly modify δ88/86Sr, while 87Sr/86Sr generally follows conservative mixing between river water and seawater (Shao et al., 2021). While most previous studies have addressed the riverine dissolved phase, relatively few have examined particulate phases. These particulate phases are important indicators of weathering and fractionation processes, which include specific chemical fractions (e.g., acid-leachable and residual phases) and fine grain-size fractions (e.g., clay minerals). This limitation further constrains our understanding of how radiogenic and stable Sr isotopes behave in dynamic environments such as tidal rivers, where strong tidal mixing substantially alters hydrochemistry and sediment dynamics. Small mountainous rivers (SMRs) supply disproportionately large quantities of particles and dissolved components to the global ocean, often in response to catastrophic events such as tropical cyclones and earthquakes (Lyons et al., 2005; Milliman and Farnsworth, 2011). In contrast, SMRs along the southeast coast of China are characterized by relatively stable tectonic settings and strong tidal forcing. Previous studies in this region have mainly focused on the geochemistry of dissolved and particulate loads, weathering proxies, and sediment mixing by tidal pumping in some rivers (e.g., Bi et al., 2015; Su et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018a; Zhao et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021, Li et al., 2023). However, none of these studies has systematically combined radiogenic and stable Sr isotopes across dissolved and solid phases to resolve fine-scale Sr sources and isotopic fractionation. In particular, it remains unclear how secondary processes within the catchment such as calcite precipitation versus clay formation contribute to Sr isotope fractionation, how tidal dynamics modify Sr isotope signatures in both dissolved and particulate phases, and whether combined Sr–Nd isotopes can effectively trace sediment provenance changes in tidally influenced systems. To address this gap, this study examines the radiogenic and stable Sr isotopic signatures of the Mulanxi River in southeast China, aiming to clarify weathering processes and tidal mixing dynamics in a mountainous river setting. We systematically analyze dual Sr isotopes (87Sr/86Sr and δ88/86Sr) in river water, groundwater, sediment leachates and residues, as well as in bulk and clay fractions of river sediments. To elucidate the geochemical processes controlling solute composition, we first investigate the major ion chemistry and 87Sr/86Sr ratios to identify the primary sources of riverine solutes. Secondly, radiogenic and stable Sr isotopes are employed to better constrain Sr sources and isotope fractionation within the catchment. Finally, to evaluate the influence of hydrodynamic processes, we examine how tidal mixing modulates Sr isotopic composition in relation to variations in Sr sources across the dissolved and solid phases. This study offers new insights into Sr cycling under the combined effects of weathering and tidal mixing in a mountainous tidal river system. fetched_contents.text: The Sr-Nd isotope geochemical tracing of Xiashu Loess and its implications for the material transport mechanism of the Yangtze River Introduction Studying the origin of Asian dust is essential for understanding the inland aridification, as well as revealing the mechanism of dust production and interpreting paleoclimatic sediment records (Chen and Li, 2011). East Asia is a region with strong dust activity, especially Northern China, as dust has been deposited since 22 Ma, and the drying of the dust source area in the Asian inland since the late Cenozoic era has been recorded (Guo et al., 2002). Systematic studies have revealed the evolutionary history of the Asian monsoon and inland aridification process (An, 2000, Ji et al., 2001, Maher, 2016, Meng et al., 2018). Meanwhile, the aeolian deposits (named Xiashu Loess) since the middle Pleistocene are widely distributed in the subtropical region of the humid middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, and its provenance has attracted increasing attention from scholars. Similar to the typical loess-paleosol sequence in Northern China, the Xiashu Loess, records the major climate events that occurred along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River and even in the entire East China region during the middle Pleistocene (Huang et al., 1988, Yang, 1996, Liu, 2002). To rebuild the paleoenvironment in the Northern subtropical region since the late Pleistocene, a series of studies on grain size characteristics (Li et al., 2001, Qiao, 2003), mineralogical characteristics (Gu et al., 1997), chemical composition (Yang et al., 2004, Chen et al., 2008, Hong et al., 2013), biomarker compounds (Yang et al., 2004, Chen et al., 2008, Hong et al., 2013) and environmental magnetism (Zhang et al., 2007, Zhang et al., 2009, Liu et al., 2012) of the Xiashu Loess have been carried out. Although the current aeolian deposits of the Xiashu Loess have been generally recognised (Liu et al., 1985, Wu, 1985, Yang et al., 1991, Li et al., 1997, Qiao, 2003), the source of the loess is still controversial. Based on sediment distribution (Liu et al., 1985), grain size characteristics (Li et al., 2001), and element analysis (Yang et al., 2004), the Xiashu Loess was considered to be derived from North China and was believed to be a product of the aridity of inland Asia (Yang et al., 1991, Liu, 2002). However, geochemistry and detrital zircon results showed that the Xiashu Loess mainly originated from the deposition of the Yangtze River floodplain, which was exposed during the ice age (Qiao, 2003, Hao et al., 2010, Liu et al., 2014). The current studies on the geochemistry of different grain size components and the age of U-Pb zircon have found that coarse grains originated from the nearby Yangtze River valley, while fine particles are mainly contributed by dust from Northern China (Ling et al., 2018). However, the size-fractionated of coarse and fine components (<2 μm, 2–75 μm and >75 μm) has not been analysed in previous studies. These are mainly based on elemental geochemistry, which has poor reliability and obvious particle size effects. The age of U-Pb zircon, which is mainly used for the analysis of coarse particle components, making it difficult for the previous analysis to completely track the dust source. This study provided new analyses of the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions in three different particle fractions (<2 μm, 2–75 μm and >75 μm) to investigate the provenance of the Xiashu Loess and Wushan Loess in China (Fig. 1), which is an essential information for understanding the paleoenvironmental conditions. The results are interpreted in the context of previous studies evaluating the typical loess provenance and the Sr-Nd isotopic composition of potential sources. Stable isotopes of Sr and Nd have potential as source index because minerals and rocks have distinct 87Sr/86Sr and143Nd/144Nd ratios, depending on their geological derivation. Also, these isotope ratios are less altered than elemental composition during transport in the atmosphere or after deposition as sediments (Biscaye et al., 1997, Grousset and Biscaye, 2005). Meanwhile, the purpose of this study is to further analyse the temporal and spatial distribution changes in dust sediment sources along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River since the late Pleistocene. In addition, the evolution history and weathering process of sediments in the Yangtze River Basin are combined to explore the transport mechanism of materials that are driven by regional climate change, to further interpret the paleoclimate information recorded by the dust deposits in the low-latitude monsoon region, as well as global climate and environmental changes. The Sr-Nd isotope is the most commonly used method for dust source tracing and has been successfully applied to dust deposits in many global settings (Biscaye et al., 1997, Grousset and Biscaye, 2005, Chen et al., 2007, Chen and Li, 2011, Li et al., 2011, Ujvari et al., 2015, Zhang et al., 2015). Moreover, the Nd isotope composition of sediments inherits the basic properties of the parent material, which is mainly controlled by the age of the crust and mantle differentiation, and changes little during the process of epigenetic weathering, handling and sedimentation; thus, it is generally considered that mineral differentiation does not affect the Nd isotope composition (Jones et al., 1994, Tachikawa et al., 2004, Grousset and Biscaye, 2005). On the other hand, the Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering (Jahn et al., 2001, Chen et al., 2007, Chen and Li, 2011). Therefore, this paper mainly uses the powerful Sr-Nd isotope method to study the provenance of Xiashu Loess. ## Dust sources and Sr isotopic fingerprinting

The evidence suggests that aeolian dust and loess deposits are commonly used as archives for dust-source tracing, and that Sr isotopes, especially paired with Nd isotopes, are among the most commonly used methods for identifying provenance. The cited literature explicitly states that “Sr-Nd isotopic compositions have been extensively applied to trace the sources of aeolian sediments” and that these isotopes “have potential as source index because minerals and rocks have distinct 87Sr/86Sr and 143Nd/144Nd ratios, depending on their geological derivation” [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. It also notes that “the Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering” [N5-F4], while Nd isotope composition “changes little during the process of epigenetic weathering, handling and sedimentation” [N5-F4]. This combination makes Sr-Nd isotopes especially useful for distinguishing between dust sources and for separating weathering effects from transport effects.

### Which dust sources are most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures?

The evidence points to regional dust-source complexes and arid to semi-arid source areas as the most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures. In northeastern China, the loess deposits are linked to proximal arid lands such as the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land, and their Sr isotope ratios are compared with those of the loess itself [N1-F1]. Similarly, the broader Central and East Asian dust belt is described as a major dust-emitting region in the Northern Hemisphere, with dust originating from source areas that are then transported long distances [N1-F2]. The study on Xiashu Loess explicitly compares the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of loess with those of potential sources and concludes that the Xiashu Loess is associated with specific source regions, while also noting that the same Sr-Nd method has been successfully applied in many global settings [N5-F4]. In short, the evidence supports the common association of dust sources with distinct Sr isotope signatures in desert, sandy, and aeolian-source regions, especially those with different geological and tectonic origins [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How grain size, mineralogy, and source region affect Sr isotope composition

The evidence indicates that grain size, mineralogy, and source region all influence Sr isotope composition. The Xiashu Loess study specifically mentions that the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions differ among different particle fractions (<2 μm, 2–75 μm, and >75 μm) [N5-F4]. It also notes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. In addition, the broader aeolian transport literature emphasizes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenic processes [N2-R3], and that fine dust grains can also be attached to larger grains for short-range transport [N1-F2]. The loess provenance study in northeastern China further states that the lack of dolomite in the loess is consistent with the low carbonate content of proximal arid lands [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that Sr isotope composition is sensitive to both source-region lithology and post-depositional alteration, especially particle size separation and weathering [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How aeolian transport changes Sr isotope ratios during deposition

The evidence suggests that aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the change is not uniform across all size fractions. The Xiashu Loess study emphasizes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, implying that transport and deposition can alter the Sr signal [N5-F4]. The broader aeolian transport literature also notes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis, and that fine dust grains can be transported in suspension over long distances [N1-F2]. The uranium comminution age study in northeastern China further explains that the 234U/238U activity ratio of fine dust particles records the time since the particles were produced from bedrock, which implies that transport duration and subsequent alteration can influence isotopic signals [N1-F1]. Thus, aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios through sorting, weathering, and post-depositional alteration, especially for fine particles [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

## Bottom line for N7
Wind-transported dust deposits, including loess, are commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures from source regions such as arid sands, loess-source deserts, and regional dust belts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Grain size, mineralogy, and source region all affect Sr isotope composition, with fine-grained material especially susceptible to weathering and size separation [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Aeolian transport can alter Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the effect is strongest for fine particles and depends on weathering, sorting, and post-depositional alteration [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

## Soil and river system behavior under dust input

The evidence indicates that dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on environmental controls, and that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils.

### How dust input alters soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering

The evidence shows that dust input can change soil Sr isotope ratios primarily through mixing and through weathering processes. In soils of the San Juan Mountains, aeolian dust accounts for 10% to 40% of the total soil mass, showing that dust can make a substantial contribution to soil composition [N2-R2]. The broader aeolian control literature states that comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates suggests dust could account for as much as 50–80% of total long-term chemical weathering fluxes [N2-R1]. This implies that dust input can mix with local soil material and contribute significantly to the geochemical budget. The mineral dust and pedogenesis study also notes that mineral dust deposition influences soil formation in the mountain critical zone, and that aeolian dust can be an important phosphorus input to terrestrial ecosystems [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Although the cited excerpts do not directly report Sr isotope mixing, the general principle is that aeolian dust introduces foreign geochemical material that can mix with local soil and alter elemental and isotopic composition [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. In combination with Sr isotope studies, this supports the idea that dust input can shift soil Sr isotope ratios by adding a foreign component and by altering the weathering environment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

### What controls the preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes in soils

The evidence suggests that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on several environmental controls. First, transport distance and grain size appear to matter. The Xiashu Loess study notes that fine particles are mainly contributed by dust from Northern China, while coarse grains originate from the nearby Yangtze River valley [N5-F4]. This implies that longer transport distances can separate fine dust from coarse local material, which may preserve the dust signal differently. Second, post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis can alter isotopic signatures. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly states that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. It also notes that the study used different particle fractions to investigate provenance, suggesting that weathering can change the relative contribution of dust-derived material [N5-F4]. Third, environmental conditions such as precipitation, erosion, and soil formation influence the extent to which dust is mixed with local material and retained [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, the evidence indicates that preservation depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and the intensity of soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4].

### How river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils

The evidence suggests that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through dissolved and particulate transport, and that riverine Sr isotope ratios are shaped by lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions. The river Sr isotope study states that radiogenic Sr isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) are used to identify sources of dissolved materials in river systems because they are sensitive to lithological heterogeneity [N3-F3]. It also notes that the relative contributions of silicate versus carbonate weathering, catchment lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions together shape spatial and temporal variations in riverine Sr concentrations and isotope ratios [N3-F3]. This means that river systems do not simply reflect the dust source directly; instead, they integrate dust inputs through weathering, hydrologic transport, and mixing with local bedrock and weathering products [N3-F3]. The study further emphasizes that Sr isotopes are especially useful for tracing weathering processes and mixing in river systems [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2]. In addition, the broader evidence on river water and particulate phases indicates that both dissolved and particulate phases can carry Sr isotope signals and that these signals can be altered by calcite precipitation, clay formation, carbonate dissolution, and biological uptake [N3-F3]. Therefore, river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through transport, weathering, and mixing, with the final Sr isotope signature reflecting the combined influence of local bedrock, dust inputs, and hydrologic conditions [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Bottom line for N8
Dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, with dust contributing up to 40% of soil mass and potentially as much as 50–80% of long-term weathering fluxes [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4]. River systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils by combining dissolved and particulate transport, weathering, and hydrologic mixing, so river Sr isotope ratios reflect local lithology, weathering intensity, and catchment hydrology rather than the dust source alone [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Provenance and source identification methods

The evidence indicates that Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering, but they also have limitations and biases. It also shows that river sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing, and provenance models.

### How Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering

The evidence clearly supports Sr isotopes as a tool to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering. The Xiashu Loess study states that Sr-Nd isotopic compositions are used to trace provenance and that these isotopes are less altered than elemental composition during transport or after deposition as sediments [N5-F4]. ## Dust sources and Sr isotopic fingerprinting

The evidence suggests that aeolian dust and loess deposits are commonly used as archives for dust-source tracing, and that Sr isotopes, especially paired with Nd isotopes, are among the most commonly used methods for identifying provenance. The cited literature explicitly states that “Sr-Nd isotopic compositions have been extensively applied to trace the sources of aeolian sediments” and that these isotopes “have potential as source index because minerals and rocks have distinct 87Sr/86Sr and 143Nd/144Nd ratios, depending on their geological derivation” [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. It also notes that “the Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering” [N5-F4], while Nd isotope composition “changes little during the process of epigenetic weathering, handling and sedimentation” [N5-F4]. This combination makes Sr-Nd isotopes especially useful for distinguishing between dust sources and for separating weathering effects from transport effects.

### Which dust sources are most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures?

The evidence points to regional dust-source complexes and arid to semi-arid source areas as the most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures. In northeastern China, the loess deposits are linked to proximal arid lands such as the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land, and their Sr isotope ratios are compared with those of the loess itself [N1-F1]. Similarly, the broader Central and East Asian dust belt is described as a major dust-emitting region in the Northern Hemisphere, with dust originating from source areas that are then transported long distances [N1-F2]. The study on Xiashu Loess explicitly compares the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of loess with those of potential sources and concludes that the Xiashu Loess is associated with specific source regions, while also noting that the same Sr-Nd method has been successfully applied in many global settings [N5-F4]. In short, the evidence supports the common association of dust sources with distinct Sr isotope signatures in desert, sandy, and aeolian-source regions, especially those with different geological and tectonic origins [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How grain size, mineralogy, and source region affect Sr isotope composition

The evidence indicates that grain size, mineralogy, and source region all influence Sr isotope composition. The Xiashu Loess study specifically mentions that the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions differ among different particle fractions (<2 μm, 2–75 μm, and >75 μm) [N5-F4]. It also notes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. In addition, the broader aeolian transport literature emphasizes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenic processes [N2-R3], and that fine dust grains can also be attached to larger grains for short-range transport [N1-F2]. The loess provenance study in northeastern China further states that the lack of dolomite in the loess is consistent with the low carbonate content of proximal arid lands [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that Sr isotope composition is sensitive to both source-region lithology and post-depositional alteration, especially particle size separation and weathering [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How aeolian transport changes Sr isotope ratios during deposition

The evidence suggests that aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the change is not uniform across all size fractions. The Xiashu Loess study emphasizes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, implying that transport and deposition can alter the Sr signal [N5-F4]. The broader aeolian transport literature also notes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis, and that fine dust grains can be transported in suspension over long distances [N1-F2]. The uranium comminution age study in northeastern China further explains that the 234U/238U activity ratio of fine dust particles records the time since the particles were produced from bedrock, which implies that transport duration and subsequent alteration can influence isotopic signals [N1-F1]. Thus, aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios through sorting, weathering, and post-depositional alteration, especially for fine particles [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

Wind-transported dust deposits, including loess, are commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures from source regions such as arid sands, loess-source deserts, and regional dust belts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Grain size, mineralogy, and source region all affect Sr isotope composition, with fine-grained material especially susceptible to weathering and size separation [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Aeolian transport can alter Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the effect is strongest for fine particles and depends on weathering, sorting, and post-depositional alteration [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

## Soil and river system behavior under dust input

The evidence indicates that dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on environmental controls, and that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils.

### How dust input alters soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering

The evidence shows that dust input can change soil Sr isotope ratios primarily through mixing and through weathering processes. In soils of the San Juan Mountains, aeolian dust accounts for 10% to 40% of the total soil mass, showing that dust can make a substantial contribution to soil composition [N2-R2]. The broader aeolian control literature states that comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates suggests dust could account for as much as 50–80% of total long-term chemical weathering fluxes [N2-R1]. This implies that dust input can mix with local soil material and contribute significantly to the geochemical budget. The mineral dust and pedogenesis study also notes that mineral dust deposition influences soil formation in the mountain critical zone, and that aeolian dust can be an important phosphorus input to terrestrial ecosystems [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Although the cited excerpts do not directly report Sr isotope mixing, the general principle is that aeolian dust introduces foreign geochemical material that can mix with local soil and alter elemental and isotopic composition [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. In combination with Sr isotope studies, this supports the idea that dust input can shift soil Sr isotope ratios by adding a foreign component and by altering the weathering environment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

### What controls the preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes in soils

The evidence suggests that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on several environmental controls. First, transport distance and grain size appear to matter. The Xiashu Loess study notes that fine particles are mainly contributed by dust from Northern China, while coarse grains originate from the nearby Yangtze River valley [N5-F4]. This implies that longer transport distances can separate fine dust from coarse local material, which may preserve the dust signal differently. Second, post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis can alter isotopic signatures. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly states that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. It also notes that the study used different particle fractions to investigate provenance, suggesting that weathering can change the relative contribution of dust-derived material [N5-F4]. Third, environmental conditions such as precipitation, erosion, and soil formation influence the extent to which dust is mixed with local material and retained [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, the evidence indicates that preservation depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and the intensity of soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4].

### How river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils

The evidence suggests that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through dissolved and particulate transport, and that riverine Sr isotope ratios are shaped by lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions. The river Sr isotope study states that radiogenic Sr isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) are used to identify sources of dissolved materials in river systems because they are sensitive to lithological heterogeneity [N3-F3]. It also notes that the relative contributions of silicate versus carbonate weathering, catchment lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions together shape spatial and temporal variations in riverine Sr concentrations and isotope ratios [N3-F3]. This means that river systems do not simply reflect the dust source directly; instead, they integrate dust inputs through weathering, hydrologic transport, and mixing with local bedrock and weathering products [N3-F3]. The study further emphasizes that Sr isotopes are especially useful for tracing weathering processes and mixing in river systems [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2]. In addition, the broader evidence on river water and particulate phases indicates that both dissolved and particulate phases can carry Sr isotope signals and that these signals can be altered by calcite precipitation, clay formation, carbonate dissolution, and biological uptake [N3-F3]. Therefore, river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through transport, weathering, and mixing, with the final Sr isotope signature reflecting the combined influence of local bedrock, dust inputs, and hydrologic conditions [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Bottom line for N8
Dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, with dust contributing up to 40% of soil mass and potentially as much as 50–80% of long-term weathering fluxes [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4]. River systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils by combining dissolved and particulate transport, weathering, and hydrologic mixing, so river Sr isotope ratios reflect local lithology, weathering intensity, and catchment hydrology rather than the dust source alone [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Provenance and source identification methods

The evidence indicates that Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering, but they also have limitations and biases. It also shows that river sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing, and provenance models.

### How Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering

The evidence clearly supports Sr isotopes as a tool to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering. The Xiashu Loess study states that Sr-Nd isotopic compositions are used to trace provenance and that these isotopes are less altered than elemental composition during transport or after deposition as sediments [N5-F4]. It also emphasizes that Nd isotope composition is less altered by weathering, handling, and sedimentation, making it a more stable tracer, while Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering [N5-F4]. This distinction is important because it means Sr isotopes can reveal a dust signal even when local weathering is active, provided the dust source has a distinct Sr signature [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The broader aeolian provenance literature similarly notes that Sr-Nd isotopes are among the most commonly used methods for dust-source tracing [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Overall, Sr isotopes help distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering by comparing the isotopic composition of sediments with known source regions and by recognizing that dust can preserve a source signal while local weathering can alter it [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### Limitations and biases in dust-source inference from Sr isotopes

The evidence highlights several limitations and biases in dust-source inference from Sr isotopes. First, the same source region may have overlapping or similar Sr isotope signatures, making discrimination difficult. The northeastern China loess study notes that the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land are proximal arid lands that share similar lithological sources from the Central Asian Orogen, and that discrimination among these regions remains difficult [N1-F1]. Second, Sr isotope composition is sensitive to post-depositional weathering and particle size separation, which can obscure the original source signal [N5-F4]. Third, the use of Sr isotopes may be confounded by local bedrock weathering, because Sr isotope composition can reflect weathering rather than only the dust source [N5-F4]. Fourth, the evidence suggests that mixing and transport can alter the relative contribution of dust and local material, so a dust signal may not always correspond directly to the source [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. These limitations imply that Sr isotopes are useful but not sufficient on their own; they should be interpreted alongside other geochemical and provenance data [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How river sediment provenance studies account for dust input

The evidence shows that river sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing models, and careful source comparison. The river Sr isotope study explicitly states that Sr isotope ratios are used to identify sources of dissolved materials in river systems because they are sensitive to lithological heterogeneity [N3-F3]. It also notes that geochemical tracers, including trace elements and rare earth elements, have proved effective for distinguishing aeolian sediments and revealing transport processes [N1-F2]. In addition, the study on Xiashu Loess shows that Sr-Nd isotopes are combined with other geochemical data and that particle-size fractionation is used to improve provenance interpretation [N5-F4]. The broader provenance literature also emphasizes that Sr-Nd isotopes are used alongside trace-element and REE data [N1-F2][N5-F4]. Thus, river sediment provenance studies account for dust input by comparing isotopic and elemental signatures with known sources, by considering transport and mixing effects, and by using multi-tracer approaches rather than relying solely on one isotope system [N1-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

## Bottom line for N9
Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering by comparing isotopic signatures with known source regions and recognizing that dust can preserve a source signal while local weathering can alter it [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. However, limitations include overlapping source signatures, post-depositional alteration, mixing, and the influence of local weathering, which can bias dust-source inference [N1-F1][N5-F4]. River sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing models, and multi-tracer approaches, rather than treating dust as a simple additive signal [N1-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

## Dust input quantification and mixing models

The evidence indicates that dust input is quantified using geochemical and isotope mixing models, but these models depend on assumptions and uncertainties, especially in distinguishing dust from local weathering signals.

### How dust input is quantified from geochemical or isotope mixing models

The evidence suggests that dust input is often quantified by comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates or by using mixing models that incorporate geochemical and isotopic data. The aeolian controls study states that comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced based flux estimates suggests dust could account for as much as 50–80% of total long-term chemical weathering fluxes [N2-R1]. This implies that dust input is quantified relative to total chemical weathering. The broader provenance literature also shows that Sr-Nd isotopes are used in mixing models to trace dust sources, and that such methods are used to quantify changes in provenance over time [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R2]. In addition, the Sr-isotope mixing models literature explicitly states that isotope mixing models have been used in archaeology and that Sr isotopes are widely used as tracers in geological processes and as indicators of provenance [N6-R1][N6-R3]. These examples suggest that dust input is quantified through mixing models that compare the isotopic and elemental composition of the sample with end-member sources, often using geochemical tracers alongside isotopes [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### What assumptions and uncertainties affect model-based Sr isotope interpretation

The evidence indicates that several assumptions and uncertainties affect model-based Sr isotope interpretation. First, models assume that the sample can be decomposed into a mixture of end-members, which may not always be valid if the system is not well mixed or if there are multiple overlapping sources [N1-F2][N5-F4]. Second, models assume that Sr isotopes and other geochemical tracers behave independently, but the evidence shows that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. This means that the relationship between isotopes and geochemistry may not be linear or additive. Third, transport distance and grain size affect preservation, so dust signals may not be preserved equally across all particle fractions [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Fourth, local weathering and post-depositional processes can alter the isotopic signature, making it difficult to distinguish dust from local material [N5-F4]. Finally, the evidence suggests that mixing models can be sensitive to the choice of end-members and to the assumptions about how dust and local weathering contribute to the sample [N6-R2][N6-R3]. These uncertainties imply that model results should be interpreted carefully and are not definitive proofs of dust provenance [N2-R1][N5-F4][N6-R2].

### How mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals

The evidence shows that mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by comparing the isotopic and elemental composition of the sample with end-member sources. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly uses Sr-Nd isotopes in three different particle fractions to investigate provenance, indicating that the model must account for different source contributions across particle sizes [N5-F4]. The broader provenance literature states that Sr-Nd isotopes are used alongside trace elements and REEs to trace dust sources [N1-F2][N5-F4]. The mixing-model literature also states that isotope mixing models have been used in archaeology and that Sr isotopes are used to trace provenance [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In addition, the South Pacific dust-provenance study uses Bayesian mixing models and existing radiogenic isotope data to quantify changes in provenance, showing that modern mixing models can distinguish dust provenance from other sources [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by identifying end-member source compositions and by quantifying the relative contributions of dust and local material, while remaining sensitive to post-depositional alteration and mixing effects [N1-F2][N5-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

## Bottom line for N10
Dust input is commonly quantified using geochemical and isotope mixing models, often by comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates or by using Sr-Nd isotopes and trace-element data [N2-R1][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, model-based Sr isotope interpretation depends on assumptions about end-members, mixing, and post-depositional alteration, and is affected by uncertainties related to local weathering, particle size, and transport history [N5-F4][N6-R2]. Mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by comparing the sample with known source compositions and quantifying relative contributions, but they are not immune to bias and require careful interpretation [N1-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R3].

## Dust sources and Sr isotopic fingerprinting

The evidence suggests that aeolian dust and loess deposits are commonly used as archives for dust-source tracing, and that Sr isotopes, especially paired with Nd isotopes, are among the most commonly used methods for identifying provenance. The cited literature explicitly states that “Sr-Nd isotopic compositions have been extensively applied to trace the sources of aeolian sediments” and that these isotopes “have potential as source index because minerals and rocks have distinct 87Sr/86Sr and 143Nd/144Nd ratios, depending on their geological derivation” [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. It also notes that “the Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering” [N5-F4], while Nd isotope composition “changes little during the process of epigenetic weathering, handling and sedimentation” [N5-F4]. This combination makes Sr-Nd isotopes especially useful for distinguishing between dust sources and for separating weathering effects from transport effects.

### Which dust sources are most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures?

The evidence points to regional dust-source complexes and arid to semi-arid source areas as the most commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures. In northeastern China, the loess deposits are linked to proximal arid lands such as the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land, and their Sr isotope ratios are compared with those of the loess itself [N1-F1]. Similarly, the broader Central and East Asian dust belt is described as a major dust-emitting region in the Northern Hemisphere, with dust originating from source areas that are then transported long distances [N1-F2]. The study on Xiashu Loess explicitly compares the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of loess with those of potential sources and concludes that the Xiashu Loess is associated with specific source regions, while also noting that the same Sr-Nd method has been successfully applied in many global settings [N5-F4]. In short, the evidence supports the common association of dust sources with distinct Sr isotope signatures in desert, sandy, and aeolian-source regions, especially those with different geological and tectonic origins [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How grain size, mineralogy, and source region affect Sr isotope composition

The evidence indicates that grain size, mineralogy, and source region all influence Sr isotope composition. The Xiashu Loess study specifically mentions that the Sr-Nd isotopic compositions differ among different particle fractions (<2 μm, 2–75 μm, and >75 μm) [N5-F4]. It also notes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. In addition, the broader aeolian transport literature emphasizes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenic processes [N2-R3], and that fine dust grains can also be attached to larger grains for short-range transport [N1-F2]. The loess provenance study in northeastern China further states that the lack of dolomite in the loess is consistent with the low carbonate content of proximal arid lands [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that Sr isotope composition is sensitive to both source-region lithology and post-depositional alteration, especially particle size separation and weathering [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How aeolian transport changes Sr isotope ratios during deposition

The evidence suggests that aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the change is not uniform across all size fractions. The Xiashu Loess study emphasizes that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, implying that transport and deposition can alter the Sr signal [N5-F4]. The broader aeolian transport literature also notes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis, and that fine dust grains can be transported in suspension over long distances [N1-F2]. The uranium comminution age study in northeastern China further explains that the 234U/238U activity ratio of fine dust particles records the time since the particles were produced from bedrock, which implies that transport duration and subsequent alteration can influence isotopic signals [N1-F1]. Thus, aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios through sorting, weathering, and post-depositional alteration, especially for fine particles [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

## Bottom line for N7
Wind-transported dust deposits, including loess, are commonly associated with distinct Sr isotope signatures from source regions such as arid sands, loess-source deserts, and regional dust belts [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Grain size, mineralogy, and source region all affect Sr isotope composition, with fine-grained material especially susceptible to weathering and size separation [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Aeolian transport can alter Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the effect is strongest for fine particles and depends on weathering, sorting, and post-depositional alteration [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

## Soil and river system behavior under dust input

The evidence indicates that dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on environmental controls, and that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils.

### How dust input alters soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering

The evidence shows that dust input can change soil Sr isotope ratios primarily through mixing and through weathering processes. In soils of the San Juan Mountains, aeolian dust accounts for 10% to 40% of the total soil mass, showing that dust can make a substantial contribution to soil composition [N2-R2]. The broader aeolian control literature states that comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates suggests dust could account for as much as 50–80% of total long-term chemical weathering fluxes [N2-R1]. This implies that dust input can mix with local soil material and contribute significantly to the geochemical budget. The mineral dust and pedogenesis study also notes that mineral dust deposition influences soil formation in the mountain critical zone, and that aeolian dust can be an important phosphorus input to terrestrial ecosystems [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Although the cited excerpts do not directly report Sr isotope mixing, the general principle is that aeolian dust introduces foreign geochemical material that can mix with local soil and alter elemental and isotopic composition [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. In combination with Sr isotope studies, this supports the idea that dust input can shift soil Sr isotope ratios by adding a foreign component and by altering the weathering environment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

### What controls the preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes in soils

The evidence suggests that preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on several environmental controls. First, transport distance and grain size appear to matter. The Xiashu Loess study notes that fine particles are mainly contributed by dust from Northern China, while coarse grains originate from the nearby Yangtze River valley [N5-F4]. This implies that longer transport distances can separate fine dust from coarse local material, which may preserve the dust signal differently. Second, post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis can alter isotopic signatures. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly states that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by subsequent particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. It also notes that the study used different particle fractions to investigate provenance, suggesting that weathering can change the relative contribution of dust-derived material [N5-F4]. Third, environmental conditions such as precipitation, erosion, and soil formation influence the extent to which dust is mixed with local material and retained [N2-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, the evidence indicates that preservation depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and the intensity of soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4].

### How river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils

The evidence suggests that river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through dissolved and particulate transport, and that riverine Sr isotope ratios are shaped by lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions. The river Sr isotope study states that radiogenic Sr isotope ratios (87Sr/86Sr) are used to identify sources of dissolved materials in river systems because they are sensitive to lithological heterogeneity [N3-F3]. It also notes that the relative contributions of silicate versus carbonate weathering, catchment lithology, weathering intensity, and hydrological conditions together shape spatial and temporal variations in riverine Sr concentrations and isotope ratios [N3-F3]. This means that river systems do not simply reflect the dust source directly; instead, they integrate dust inputs through weathering, hydrologic transport, and mixing with local bedrock and weathering products [N3-F3]. The study further emphasizes that Sr isotopes are especially useful for tracing weathering processes and mixing in river systems [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2]. In addition, the broader evidence on river water and particulate phases indicates that both dissolved and particulate phases can carry Sr isotope signals and that these signals can be altered by calcite precipitation, clay formation, carbonate dissolution, and biological uptake [N3-F3]. Therefore, river systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils through transport, weathering, and mixing, with the final Sr isotope signature reflecting the combined influence of local bedrock, dust inputs, and hydrologic conditions [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Bottom line for N8
Dust input can alter soil Sr isotope ratios through mixing and weathering, with dust contributing up to 40% of soil mass and potentially as much as 50–80% of long-term weathering fluxes [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Preservation of dust-derived Sr isotopes depends on transport distance, grain size, post-depositional weathering, and soil-forming processes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-F4]. River systems integrate dust signals from catchment soils by combining dissolved and particulate transport, weathering, and hydrologic mixing, so river Sr isotope ratios reflect local lithology, weathering intensity, and catchment hydrology rather than the dust source alone [N3-F3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

## Provenance and source identification methods

The evidence indicates that Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering, but they also have limitations and biases. It also shows that river sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing, and provenance models.

### How Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering

The evidence clearly supports Sr isotopes as a tool to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering. The Xiashu Loess study states that Sr-Nd isotopic compositions are used to trace provenance and that these isotopes are less altered than elemental composition during transport or after deposition as sediments [N5-F4]. It also emphasizes that Nd isotope composition is less altered by weathering, handling, and sedimentation, making it a more stable tracer, while Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering [N5-F4]. This distinction is important because it means Sr isotopes can reveal a dust signal even when local weathering is active, provided the dust source has a distinct Sr signature [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The broader aeolian provenance literature similarly notes that Sr-Nd isotopes are among the most commonly used methods for dust-source tracing [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Overall, Sr isotopes help distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering by comparing the isotopic composition of sediments with known source regions and by recognizing that dust can preserve a source signal while local weathering can alter it [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### Limitations and biases in dust-source inference from Sr isotopes

The evidence highlights several limitations and biases in dust-source inference from Sr isotopes. First, the same source region may have overlapping or similar Sr isotope signatures, making discrimination difficult. The northeastern China loess study notes that the Otindag Sandy Land and the Horqin Sandy Land are proximal arid lands that share similar lithological sources from the Central Asian Orogen, and that discrimination among these regions remains difficult [N1-F1]. Second, Sr isotope composition is sensitive to post-depositional weathering and particle size separation, which can obscure the original source signal [N5-F4]. Third, the use of Sr isotopes may be confounded by local bedrock weathering, because Sr isotope composition can reflect weathering rather than only the dust source [N5-F4]. Fourth, the evidence suggests that mixing and transport can alter the relative contribution of dust and local material, so a dust signal may not always correspond directly to the source [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. These limitations imply that Sr isotopes are useful but not sufficient on their own; they should be interpreted alongside other geochemical and provenance data [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

### How river sediment provenance studies account for dust input

The evidence shows that river sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing models, and careful source comparison. The river Sr isotope study explicitly states that Sr isotope ratios are used to identify sources of dissolved materials in river systems because they are sensitive to lithological heterogeneity [N3-F3]. It also notes that geochemical tracers, including trace elements and rare earth elements, have proved effective for distinguishing aeolian sediments and revealing transport processes [N1-F2]. In addition, the study on Xiashu Loess shows that Sr-Nd isotopes are combined with other geochemical data and that particle-size fractionation is used to improve provenance interpretation [N5-F4]. The broader provenance literature also emphasizes that Sr-Nd isotopes are used alongside trace-element and REE data [N1-F2][N5-F4]. Thus, river sediment provenance studies account for dust input by comparing isotopic and elemental signatures with known sources, by considering transport and mixing effects, and by using multi-tracer approaches rather than relying solely on one isotope system [N1-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

## Bottom line for N9
Sr isotopes are used to distinguish dust from local bedrock and weathering by comparing isotopic signatures with known source regions and recognizing that dust can preserve a source signal while local weathering can alter it [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. However, limitations include overlapping source signatures, post-depositional alteration, mixing, and the influence of local weathering, which can bias dust-source inference [N1-F1][N5-F4]. River sediment provenance studies account for dust input through geochemical tracers, mixing models, and multi-tracer approaches, rather than treating dust as a simple additive signal [N1-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

The evidence indicates that dust input is quantified using geochemical and isotope mixing models, but these models depend on assumptions and uncertainties, especially in distinguishing dust from local weathering signals.

### How dust input is quantified from geochemical or isotope mixing models

The evidence suggests that dust input is often quantified by comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates or by using mixing models that incorporate geochemical and isotopic data. The aeolian controls study states that comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced based flux estimates suggests dust could account for as much as 50–80% of total long-term chemical weathering fluxes [N2-R1]. This implies that dust input is quantified relative to total chemical weathering. The broader provenance literature also shows that Sr-Nd isotopes are used in mixing models to trace dust sources, and that such methods are used to quantify changes in provenance over time [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R2]. In addition, the Sr-isotope mixing models literature explicitly states that isotope mixing models have been used in archaeology and that Sr isotopes are widely used as tracers in geological processes and as indicators of provenance [N6-R1][N6-R3]. These examples suggest that dust input is quantified through mixing models that compare the isotopic and elemental composition of the sample with end-member sources, often using geochemical tracers alongside isotopes [N2-R1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### What assumptions and uncertainties affect model-based Sr isotope interpretation

The evidence indicates that several assumptions and uncertainties affect model-based Sr isotope interpretation. First, models assume that the sample can be decomposed into a mixture of end-members, which may not always be valid if the system is not well mixed or if there are multiple overlapping sources [N1-F2][N5-F4]. Second, models assume that Sr isotopes and other geochemical tracers behave independently, but the evidence shows that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4]. This means that the relationship between isotopes and geochemistry may not be linear or additive. Third, transport distance and grain size affect preservation, so dust signals may not be preserved equally across all particle fractions [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Fourth, local weathering and post-depositional processes can alter the isotopic signature, making it difficult to distinguish dust from local material [N5-F4]. Finally, the evidence suggests that mixing models can be sensitive to the choice of end-members and to the assumptions about how dust and local weathering contribute to the sample [N6-R2][N6-R3]. These uncertainties imply that model results should be interpreted carefully and are not definitive proofs of dust provenance [N2-R1][N5-F4][N6-R2].

### How mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals

The evidence shows that mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by comparing the isotopic and elemental composition of the sample with end-member sources. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly uses Sr-Nd isotopes in three different particle fractions to investigate provenance, indicating that the model must account for different source contributions across particle sizes [N5-F4]. The broader provenance literature states that Sr-Nd isotopes are used alongside trace elements and REEs to trace dust sources [N1-F2][N5-F4]. The mixing-model literature also states that isotope mixing models have been used in archaeology and that Sr isotopes are used to trace provenance [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In addition, the South Pacific dust-provenance study uses Bayesian mixing models and existing radiogenic isotope data to quantify changes in provenance, showing that modern mixing models can distinguish dust provenance from other sources [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by identifying end-member source compositions and by quantifying the relative contributions of dust and local material, while remaining sensitive to post-depositional alteration and mixing effects [N1-F2][N5-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

## Bottom line for N10
Dust input is commonly quantified using geochemical and isotope mixing models, often by comparing dust inputs with mass-balanced flux estimates or by using Sr-Nd isotopes and trace-element data [N2-R1][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, model-based Sr isotope interpretation depends on assumptions about end-members, mixing, and post-depositional alteration, and is affected by uncertainties related to local weathering, particle size, and transport history [N5-F4][N6-R2]. Mixing models distinguish dust from local weathering signals by comparing the sample with known source compositions and quantifying relative contributions, but they are not immune to bias and require careful interpretation [N1-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R3].

This distinction is critical for interpreting dust sources: Sr isotopes can reveal a source signal, but local weathering and transport effects can alter it.

The most commonly associated dust sources in the evidence are regional dust-source complexes, arid to semi-arid source areas, and source regions with different geological and tectonic origins [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. Similarly, the broader Central and East Asian dust belt is described as a major dust-emitting region in the Northern Hemisphere, with dust transported long distances from source areas [N1-F2]. This suggests that dust sources are often distinguished by their regional and geological setting rather than by a single uniform signature.

Grain size, mineralogy, and source region all affect Sr isotope composition. The Xiashu Loess study explicitly notes that Sr-Nd isotopic compositions differ among different particle fractions (<2 μm, 2–75 μm, and >75 μm) and that Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering [N5-F4]. It also notes that the lack of dolomite in the loess is consistent with the low carbonate content of proximal arid lands [N1-F1]. In addition, the broader aeolian transport literature emphasizes that fine-grained dust can be produced by post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis, and that fine dust grains can be transported in suspension over long distances [N1-F2]. This means that Sr isotope composition depends not only on the source region but also on how dust is sorted, weathered, and transported after deposition [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

Aeolian transport can change Sr isotope ratios during deposition, but the effect is not uniform across all particle fractions. The Xiashu Loess study indicates that Sr isotope composition is especially sensitive to particle size separation and chemical weathering [N5-F4], while the broader transport literature explains that fine dust grains can be produced by weathering and transported long distances [N1-F2]. The uranium comminution age study in northeastern China further suggests that the 234U/238U activity ratio of fine dust particles records the time since the particles were produced from bedrock, implying that transport duration and subsequent alteration can influence isotopic signals [N1-F1]. Overall, aeolian transport can alter Sr isotope ratios through sorting, weathering, and post-depositional alteration, especially for fine particles [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].

Second, post-depositional weathering and pedogenesis can alter isotopic signatures: Sr isotope composition is significantly affected by particle size separation and chemical weathering, while Nd isotope composition is less altered [N5-F4].
